hints: Notice the y-axis is distance travelled, not distance from home - it cannot decrease when the student cycles back.
Check the three time intervals: 10 minutes uphill to $1 \text{ km}$, then 5 minutes stopped, then the return journey.
Connect twice the speed to the gradient: on a distance-time graph gradient is speed, so the final section must be steeper and take half the outward time.
walkthrough: Identify the quantity: distance travelled always increases or stays constant, so the graph can never slope downwards to zero. This rules out a displacement-time shape.
First stage is 0 to 10 minutes cycling to the shop $1 \text{ km}$ away, so distance travelled rises from $0$ to $1 \text{ km}$ with constant gradient.
Second stage is 5 minutes in the shop from 10 to 15 minutes, so distance travelled stays at $1 \text{ km}$ and the graph is horizontal.
Return speed is twice the outward speed, so for the same $1 \text{ km}$ the time is halved: $10/2 = 5$ minutes, from 15 to 20 minutes.
On a distance-time graph speed is gradient $v = \Delta s / \Delta t$, so the last section from $1 \text{ km}$ to $2 \text{ km}$ must be steeper than the first section. This is option D.

options.A: Shows displacement from home returning to zero, not distance travelled, and uses 5 minutes uphill instead of 10 minutes.
options.B: Shows displacement from home returning to zero at 20 minutes, whereas distance travelled must keep increasing.
options.C: Shows distance travelled increasing to $2 \text{ km}$ but uses 5 minutes uphill and 5 minutes in shop from 5 to 10 minutes, not the given times.
options.D: Shows distance travelled rising to $1 \text{ km}$ in 10 minutes, flat for 5 minutes, then rising more steeply to $2 \text{ km}$ in 5 minutes.
